summary: The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol measures one-way network characteristics such as delay and loss. Precise one-way measurement became practical with good time sources such as GPS, and OWAMP lets different implementations interoperate. It was later updated by RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545.

eli5.summary: To learn how long a letter takes to get there, not there and back, both clocks must agree. This lets two computers test one direction at a time.

questions: how to measure one-way packet loss
how does owamp measure one-way delay
subtitle: A standard way to ask two hosts to measure one-way delay and loss between them, in one direction at a time.

tldr.problem: Metrics for one-way delay and loss existed, but there was no standard for starting test streams or exchanging packets, so different measurement platforms could not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: OWAMP-Control runs over TCP to set up, start and stop sessions and fetch results. OWAMP-Test sends timestamped UDP packets on a schedule both ends can reproduce, with optional authentication and encryption.
tldr.outcome: It gave one-way active measurement a common protocol, with the stated hope of making one-way delay as commonplace to measure as round-trip time with ping. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545.

today: RFC 4656 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545. See RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545 for those changes.

sections.title: The Problem and the Goals
sections.content:
The IETF IP Performance Metrics working group had defined metrics for one-way packet delay (RFC 2679) and loss (RFC 2680). Several platforms collected them, but there was no standard way to start a test stream or exchange packets interoperably. Cheap GPS and CDMA time sources, or proximity to NTP stratum 1 servers, were making accurate clocks common enough to make the idea practical.

The authors list further goals: tests that are hard to detect and manipulate, security, a clean split between control and test functions, and support for small test packets. Test traffic is just a stream of UDP packets to negotiated ports with negotiated sizes, so there may be nothing static in the packets. An encrypted mode makes it impossible to alter timestamps undetectably.
sections.eli5: Measuring one direction needs very accurate clocks, and those are now cheap. This protocol lets different machines agree on how to run such a test.

sections.title: Two Protocols and Five Roles
sections.content:
OWAMP is really two protocols. OWAMP-Control initiates, starts and stops test sessions and fetches their results. OWAMP-Test exchanges the test packets. The RFC bundles both on purpose, to encourage OWAMP-Control as a common denominator, but it neither anticipates nor recommends it as the basis for a general-purpose measurement control protocol.

The document separates five logical roles: Session-Sender, Session-Receiver, Server, Control-Client and Fetch-Client. One host can play several roles. In the common two-host case, one host is Control-Client, Fetch-Client and Session-Sender, and the other is Server and Session-Receiver. OWAMP-Control is layered over TCP and OWAMP-Test over UDP. The client connects to well-known TCP port 861, and the connection stays open for the test sessions.
sections.eli5: One conversation is for planning the test, like two friends agreeing by phone to race. The other is the race itself. Each friend can play several parts.

sections.title: Connection Setup and Modes
sections.content:
After the TCP connection opens, the server sends a greeting with a Modes field. Three modes exist: unauthenticated (value 1), authenticated (2) and encrypted (4). The server ORs together the modes it supports; the first 29 bits MUST be zero and are the only intended extension mechanism. The greeting also carries a random 16-octet Challenge, a 16-octet Salt and a Count for key derivation. Count MUST be a power of 2 and at least 1024. A Modes value of zero means the server does not want to talk.

The client replies with a Set-Up-Response holding its chosen mode, a KeyID naming a shared secret, a Token and a Client-IV. The shared secret is a passphrase turned into a key with PBKDF2 using HMAC-SHA1. The token holds the challenge, a 16-octet AES session key and a 32-octet HMAC-SHA1 session key, encrypted with AES in CBC mode. The server answers with Server-Start, whose Accept field is zero if it will continue.

In authenticated and encrypted modes, which behave the same for OWAMP-Control, every later message is encrypted with AES in CBC mode and carries an HMAC, which is HMAC-SHA1 truncated to 128 bits (16 octets).
sections.eli5: Before talking, the server says which kinds of secret handshake it knows. The client picks one and proves it knows the shared password without saying it out loud.

sections.title: Running Test Sessions
sections.content:
A client sends zero or more Request-Session messages, and the server answers each with Accept-Session. A request names the IP version, sender and receiver addresses and ports, the number of packets, a start time, padding length, and a Timeout: a packet not received within that many seconds of being sent counts as lost. A Type-P descriptor can ask for a DSCP value or a PHB identification code, and all zeros means default best-effort service. Flags tell the server whether to configure the sender, the receiver or both. A server can refuse, and it SHOULD keep the TCP connection open when it does.

The client then sends Start-Sessions and the server replies Start-Ack. While sessions run, only Stop-Sessions is allowed, and either side may send it. It carries, for each session, the next sequence number and any skip ranges, which are packets the sender never sent, for example because it started too late. A sender MUST NOT send a packet whose scheduled time is more than Timeout in the past.

Results are retrieved with Fetch-Session, which names a session by its 16-octet session identifier (SID) and a range of sequence numbers. Each packet record is 25 octets and holds a sequence number, send and receive timestamps with error estimates, and the TTL or Hop Limit. A lost packet is recorded with a zero receive timestamp and a TTL of 255.
sections.eli5: The client says how many test packets to send and when. After the test, it can come back and ask for the score card, which lists every packet and whether it arrived.

sections.title: OWAMP-Test Packets
sections.content:
Each test packet is a UDP datagram with a sequence number starting at zero, a timestamp, an error estimate and optional padding. The sender SHOULD set the IPv4 TTL, or IPv6 Hop Limit, to 255. The timestamp uses the NTP format from RFC 1305: 32 bits of seconds since 0h on 1 January 1900, then 32 bits of fraction. The error estimate has an S bit (set if the clock is synchronized to UTC from an external source), a Scale and a Multiplier, and the error is Multiplier times 2^-32 times 2^Scale seconds. A Multiplier of zero means the packet should be discarded.

The minimum data segment is 14 octets in unauthenticated mode and 48 octets in the other two modes. Authenticated mode encrypts only the first 16-octet block (AES ECB) and leaves the timestamp in clear text, which saves time between reading the clock and sending. Encrypted mode encrypts the first two blocks with AES CBC, protecting the timestamp as well. Test keys are derived from the control session keys and the SID, and no chaining spans packets, so lost, duplicated or reordered packets do not break decryption.

The receiver timestamps each packet and records sequence number, send time, receive time and TTL. Duplicates MUST be recorded, because the protocol has to be able to measure duplication. Packets failing HMAC verification, or with implausible send timestamps, MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: Each test packet is a postcard stamped with the exact time it left, plus a note on how accurate that clock is. The receiver stamps it again on arrival, and the difference is the trip time.

sections.title: Send Schedules and Random Numbers
sections.content:
Sender and receiver must know exactly when each packet was supposed to leave, so the receiver can place lost packets in time. The schedule is a list of slots. A type 0 slot waits an exponentially distributed random time with a given mean, then sends. A type 1 slot waits a fixed time, then sends. The list repeats. A single type 0 slot gives a Poisson stream, a single type 1 slot gives a periodic stream, and a type 0 slot with a non-zero parameter followed by a type 1 slot with a zero parameter gives a Poisson stream of back-to-back pairs.

Both ends must compute identical random values, and ordinary math libraries differ in how they compute logarithms. So the RFC specifies Algorithm S from Knuth, which avoids logarithms, using 64-bit integer arithmetic and fixed constants. Uniform random inputs come from AES in counter mode, with the SID as the seed. This is why even a server that supports only unauthenticated mode MUST include AES.
sections.eli5: Both computers need the same secret shuffle for when to send packets, so the receiver can tell which ones went missing. They use a shared recipe so their random choices come out the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authenticated mode is meant to prevent theft of service, and to stop an attacker who cannot read the test traffic from tampering with results. Encrypted mode aims to make it hard for someone in the middle to make results look better than they are. To prevent third-party denial of service, servers MUST by default decline requests whose receiver address is not the control connection's source or an address the server controls, and test packets MUST NOT use spoofed source addresses.

Servers MUST limit network capacity and memory use, with conservative defaults. The RFC explains why it avoided TLS, DTLS and IPsec: stream-based TLS does not suit lossy UDP test packets, DTLS anti-replay would hide the duplication and reordering OWAMP wants to measure, and IPsec cannot protect part of a packet, which authenticated mode needs. New ciphers can be introduced through the Modes bits, though that scheme is open to downgrade attacks. Key management is manual, with long-term keys per user. HMAC verification MUST succeed before a message is used.
sections.eli5: The protocol has a lock so strangers cannot misuse the server or fake the results. It also has limits so nobody can use the server to flood somebody else.
